title: AI reads and sorts incoming IRS and state tax notices
problem: Tax notices are technical, carry strict deadlines, and working out what changed and how to respond takes longer than expected and varies by practitioner.
approach: An uploaded notice is analysed to extract the deadline, amount due and issue and list response paths (Wolters Kluwer, Thomson Reuters tools).
Vendor says this shortens the time from receipt to action (vendor-published; no figure).
The practitioner checks the extracted deadline, amount and issue against the notice; the reviewer chooses the course of action.

title: AI drafts client explanations and formal replies to tax notices
problem: Once a notice is understood, the firm must explain it to the client in plain language and prepare a formal response, usually drafted from scratch each time.
approach: The tool drafts a client-ready explanation and an agency response, such as a penalty abatement request (Wolters Kluwer, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel Tax).
EY's survey says respondents automate or partly automate responses to tax authority enquiries (vendor-published).
The practitioner verifies numbers, deadline and substantiation and signs as the owner of the position.
who: Wolters Kluwer, Thomson Reuters, Blue J, EY

title: Weekly IRS transcript checks to act before underreporter notices arrive
problem: The IRS underreporter flag appears on an account transcript before the CP2000 letter, but few practitioners check transcripts, so clients are surprised and penalties and interest accrue.
approach: A practitioner pulls account transcripts for about 700 clients weekly with third-party software, which highlights transcripts carrying the underreporting flag.
He compares the return with IRS wage and income data, amends if needed, and can tell the IRS the error was self-discovered.
700 clients monitored weekly; he says this avoids penalties and interest (self-reported). The professional decides whether to amend.

title: Pre-filing review that reconciles returns to third-party data and flags audit risks
problem: IRS data matching flags mismatches between returns and third-party reports, so a technically correct return can still draw a notice if numbers do not visibly reconcile.
approach: Before sign-off, AI reviews a return 'as though it were a partner-level signer' (Wolters Kluwer), listing risks and a must-fix list.
Practitioner commentary recommends reconciliation checklists, documented review trails and written business purpose; no outcome published for any tool.
The reviewer investigates each flagged item, decides what substantiation to request and signs the return.

title: Checking transfer pricing files against public data to anticipate challenge
problem: Authorities use technology to review documentation, and inconsistencies between transfer pricing files and public data can invite challenge.
approach: EY describes TP Doc Insights, a GenAI tool that finds discrepancies between existing documentation and public data (vendor-published; announced).
KPMG says GenAI can help in transfer pricing controversy by reviewing historical documents and formulating responses.
Transfer pricing professionals review flagged discrepancies. No outcome published.

title: In-house tax teams summarise legislation and dispute files with AI
problem: Controversy teams hold large volumes of internal opinions and memos, must track proposed legislation, and need data given to different authorities to be consistent.
approach: EY's survey says respondents use or expect to use GenAI to summarise tax information and make data shared with authorities consistent.
39% built a tax risk or controversy pilot or tool (vendor-published survey); 46% very satisfied versus 31%, in a self-selected sample.
EY says agentic outputs should be reviewed by humans.

title: Agents draft replies to audit queries and track document requests
problem: During an examination the taxpayer answers a stream of formal records requests under deadlines, while some authorities arrive at audits with transaction data already analysed.
approach: EY authors say tax agents can draft responses to audit queries; survey respondents automate or partly automate them.
A Miller & Chevalier seminar covered AI in tax controversy; EY India announced an AI Tax Hub with litigation agents.
EY authors: AI should improve the human's review, not remove it. No outcome published.

title: AI drafting for Tax Court and IRS filings, with citation checks
problem: Counsel and self-represented taxpayers use general models to draft filings, but models can invent citations; in Clinco v. Commissioner three of four cited cases were apparently invented.
approach: Use is documented mainly through failures; the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility recommends written AI policies and treating AI text as draft.
Independent counts: about 2,200 decisions worldwide involve hallucinated authorities, 25 tagged tax; one Tax Court judge saw fewer than a dozen.
The signing practitioner independently verifies facts, authorities, citations and calculations; briefs get a second reviewer or citation log.
who: Tax Court cases, IRS OPR, Journal of Accountancy

title: Idea: counsel-directed enterprise AI analysis to protect legal privilege
problem: Idea, not a deployment: in United States v. Heppner (17 Feb 2026) AI reports made with a consumer tool without counsel's direction were held not privileged.
approach: Law-firm guidance advises treating public AI tools as third parties, using enterprise tools with limits on training and retention, and logging outputs.
Miller & Chevalier's Sheri Dillon names AI ethics, privilege and confidentiality as a top 2026 challenge.
Counsel decides what is run through AI and directs it, documenting that direction.

title: Idea: value-based pricing for AI-speeded controversy work
problem: Idea, not a deployment: the IRS says billing for manual time not spent may breach Circular 230, and AI savings should be passed on.
approach: The AICPA asked the IRS for clarification, saying the guidance does not appear to allow value pricing and overlooks implementation risk.
No firm is named as having changed its fee basis for controversy work.
The practitioner decides fee basis and disclosure.

title: Idea: risk-register checks before deploying AI in tax practice (Werfel framework)
problem: Idea, not a deployment: tax practitioners and administrators do not know which questions to ask to assess AI readiness or vet vendors.
approach: Danny Werfel's framework (31 Aug 2026, via the AICPA) gives risk registers for authorities (20) and preparers (15) and an eight-step method.
The AICPA launched the Council on AI Risk in Tax on 23 Sep 2026 to test and refine it.
Tier 1 risks must be addressed before launch; human approval of irreversible or financial agent actions is an illustrative control.

title: Idea: preventive controls and real-time data exchange instead of audit defence
problem: Idea, not a deployment: Deloitte says real-time, data-driven authorities may mean more granular requests and more audits, making reactive issue management unsustainable.
approach: Deloitte says companies would need upstream data quality and preventive controls built into processes; EY says real-time interactions may reduce flash points.
OECD commissioners agreed in November 2025 to move to pilots of real-time automated information sharing. Both firm pieces are discussion, not deployments.
Deloitte says human judgment remains instrumental and experts validate AI outputs.

title: IRS machine learning picks returns and issues to examine
problem: The IRS must choose which returns to examine with too few examiners; older scoring produced many no-change audits, and the first contact is a model-driven selection with undisclosed reasons.
approach: The IRS added machine learning to return and issue selection, including a Line Anomaly Recommender and a Form 1040 issue-suggesting model.
TIGTA found the IRS lacks sufficient processes to evaluate whether the models beat prior processes (independent).
Human classifiers review recommender output before returns go to the field; examiners can add or remove suggested issues.

title: Idea: feedback, drift and fairness testing for audit-selection models
problem: Idea, not a deployment: selection models are not routinely tuned on exam results, and researchers estimated Black taxpayers were audited at 2.9 to 4.7 times the rate of others.
approach: Compare model-suggested issues with those examiners pursued, track no-change rates and drift, and test models against group outcomes; no implementation is published.
GAO-reported gaps: 4 of 5 high-impact IRS AI uses lacked testing documentation; 2 of 5 lacked an impact assessment (independent).
TIGTA recommended exam results feed model monitoring; the IRS agreed, subject to staffing and Treasury guidance.

title: AI risk targeting for audits at other tax authorities
problem: Authorities need to find inaccuracies and fraud across huge return populations with limited audit staff, and taxpayers face selection by models with unpublished criteria.
approach: HMRC says AI and analytics highlight possibly inaccurate returns; Austria has used machine-learning risk models since 2014; California since 2021.
HMRC reports GBP 10 billion protected or recovered in 2025-26 (self-reported); Austria reports about EUR 185 million additional revenue (self-reported).
HMRC says skilled caseworkers make final decisions; Austrian flagged cases go to staff.
who: HMRC, Austria, Hungary, California, South Carolina

title: IRS AI fraud and identity-theft screening that pauses refunds
problem: Refund fraud and identity theft at scale cannot be screened by hand, but a held refund creates a taxpayer problem ending in calls and verification.
approach: IRS models score returns for risk; GAO found two uses automating decisions, including pausing refunds that look like identity theft.
After a pause, an employee reviews the risk factors and decides whether to release the refund.
GAO counted 18 of 43 use cases operational (independent); it did not measure detection accuracy.

title: AI and automation speed IRS amended-return processing
problem: The IRS receives about 5 million amended returns a year, and backlogs push taxpayers into correspondence, calls and disputes.
approach: The IRS CIO told employees AI is speeding processing of hundreds of thousands of amended returns; the method is not described.
Processing time fell from 12, 14 or 16 weeks to under three days (self-reported).
Human checkpoints are not described in the source.

title: Voice and chat bots answering taxpayer calls, questions and payment plans
problem: Phone demand at the IRS far exceeds live-assistor capacity, and with staffing about 25% lower the IRS expects to rely more on technology.
approach: The IRS runs chatbots and voicebots for tax questions and payment plans; its June 2025 inventory lists 11 voicebots and two chatbots.
Filing season 2026: 17% completed in the voicebot, about 46% transferred to an assistor (independent); sessions reached nearly 25 million (self-reported).
Callers can ask for a live assistor; over 85% who chose a callback reached one.

title: Real-time prompts asking taxpayers to check unusual entries (Australia)
problem: Errors found after lodgment become reviews, notices, amendments and disputes; catching them at filing is cheaper for both sides.
approach: ATO models in myTax compare entered amounts with similar taxpayers or prior years and prompt the taxpayer to check specific items.
More than 636,000 prompts, protecting about AUD 78.9 million (2023-24) (self-reported).
The taxpayer decides what to amend; the ATO says decisions adversely affecting rights are made by a human.

title: AI assistants for tax-authority service staff
problem: Authority phone staff must find the right guidance while a caller waits, and wrong or slow answers feed later notices and disputes.
approach: The IRS rolled out Archie for researching the Internal Revenue Manual; California's CDTFA launched a GenAI answer-drafting tool on 22 August 2025.
HMRC is piloting AI call summaries for human review; France uses AI to draft replies that staff validate.
HMRC reports over 28,000 Copilot licences by March 2026 (self-reported). The representative or agent decides what to use.

title: Examiner and caseworker assistants that sort evidence and draft documents
problem: Auditors and caseworkers must sort large volumes of receipts, invoices and case documents and draft routine requests and reports, with fewer staff.
approach: The ATO built AI that matches substantiation documents to claims and orders them for auditors; HMRC is trialling Copilot for caseworkers.
ATO says the assistant saves time and makes claims easier to assess (self-reported; no figure).
ATO auditors decide deduction validity; IRS agents reportedly review drafts (EisnerAmper, unconfirmed by IRS); TAS staff verify AI content.
who: ATO, HMRC, IRS, Taxpayer Advocate Service

title: AI agents for case summaries and search in IRS legal units
problem: Chief Counsel, Appeals and the Taxpayer Advocate handle document-heavy cases with reduced staff; the IRS workforce fell by about 25% in 2025.
approach: Salesforce said Agentforce would be used across the Office of Chief Counsel, TAS and Appeals for case summaries and search (announced).
The vendor says the agents cannot make final decisions or disburse funds; the stated aim is faster case completion (vendor-published).
Staff make the decisions.

title: Machine-learning grouping and routing of tax-appeal files (Brazil)
problem: Brazil had around USD 140 billion in assessed taxes awaiting administrative appeal decisions, and an appeal ruling took about six years.
approach: Under the AI Litigation Project, supervised machine learning groups similar appeal files so they go to the same officers.
First trials showed over 80% sensitivity and specificity (self-reported; a model accuracy measure, not a speed outcome).
Appeal officers handle files and rulings, and label files to improve later suggestions.

title: Announced agentic case management for tax-authority casework
problem: Case work is information-heavy, and isolated experiments risk duplication and weak assurance; HMRC aims for at least 90% digital interactions by 2030.
approach: The ATO prioritised seven enterprise AI use cases, including case profiling assistants, triage of taxpayer requests and drafting position papers (announced).
HMRC's roadmap, as summarised by ICAS, names agentic AI for case management and plans generative AI to summarise case documents.
ATO says decisions remain with people and drafts stay subject to human review. No outcome published.

title: Idea: AI reasoning to detect and analyse abusive tax strategies
problem: Idea, not a deployment: well-advised taxpayers design tax-minimisation strategies that are hard for authorities to find and analyse across statutes, case law and guidance.
approach: Researchers tested advanced LLMs on interpreting, verifying and generating tax strategies, and report LLM reasoning found an apparently novel strategy (independent).
A paper with overlapping authors pairs LLMs with a symbolic solver to improve auditability.
Human checkpoints are not described; this is an academic experiment.
